overview: Object Oriented Programming (OOP) is a programming paradigm that organizes programs as collections of objects, each representing an instance of a class. It's a way to structure and organize code to make it more reusable and maintainable.

sections.explanation: Abstraction is the concept of showing only the necessary information to the outside world, hiding the internal implementation details.
sections.analogy: Think of a car's engine - you don't need to know how it works to drive it.
sections.example: A bank account class might only show the account balance, hiding the internal calculations.

sections.explanation: Encapsulation is the concept of bundling data and methods that operate on that data within a single unit, making it harder to access or modify the data directly.
sections.analogy: Think of a safe - you can't just open it and take the money, you need the combination.
sections.example: A person class might encapsulate their name, age, and address, making it harder to access or modify these attributes directly.

sections.explanation: Inheritance is the concept of creating a new class that is a modified version of an existing class, inheriting its properties and methods.
sections.analogy: Think of a child inheriting traits from their parents - they get the good and the bad!
sections.example: A Dog class might inherit from an Animal class, inheriting its basic characteristics.
key_points: Creates a new class based on an existing one

sections.explanation: Polymorphism is the concept of having multiple forms or behaviors of a class, depending on the context.
sections.analogy: Think of a shape that can be a circle, square, or triangle, depending on how you look at it.
sections.example: A Shape class might have different behaviors depending on its type (e.g., drawing a circle or a square).

sections.explanation: Interfaces are abstract classes that define a contract or set of methods that must be implemented by any class that implements it.
sections.analogy: Think of a recipe book - it defines what a cake should look like, but doesn't tell you how to make it.
sections.example: A Printable interface might define methods for printing, and a Document class might implement it.
key_points: Defines a contract or set of methods
Must be implemented by any class that implements it

teaching_tips: Focus on understanding the concepts, not just the syntax
Use analogies to help illustrate complex ideas
Practice, practice, practice - the best way to learn OOP is by doing it!
